questions.problem:
Consider the matrix $K$ for which ${\lambda }_{1}=2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-5$ are eigenvalues, and

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]
$$

are the respective eigenvectors. What are the values of $a,b,c$ given that

$$
K=[\begin{aligned}b & 1 \\ 0 & c\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & a\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}b & 1 \\ 0 & c\end{aligned}]}^{-1}?
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-5,$ we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -5\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns: 

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=2,$ and

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=-5.$

Therefore, we get

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
K=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -5\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}.
$$

 

In conclusion, we get  $a=-5,$ $b=-1,$ and $c=-1.$

questions.worked_solution:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 15\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns: 

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=3,$ and

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=15.$

Therefore, we get

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}].

Finally, we obtain

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 15\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}.

questions.problem:
Determine if the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ -3 & 4\end{aligned}]$
is diagonalizable or not, and if it is diagonalizable, find a corresponding diagonal matrix $D.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ by solving $det(A-\lambda I)=0$:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}-2-\lambda  & 3 \\ -3 & 4-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-2-\lambda )(4-\lambda )-(3)(-3) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda +1 & =0 \\ (\lambda -1)(\lambda -1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=1.$ Since we get one repeated eigenvalue, the matrix might not be diagonalizable. To check this, we row-reduce the matrix $(A-1I)\text{x}=0:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}A-1I & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ -3 & 4\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 \\ -3 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has only $1$ pivot column. This implies that we will have only $2-1=1$ linearly independent eigenvector corresponding to the current eigenvalue. Therefore, $A$ is not diagonalizable.

questions.problem:
Determine if the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}8 & 9 \\ -4 & -4\end{aligned}]$
is diagonalizable or not, and if it is diagonalizable, find a corresponding diagonal matrix $D.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ by solving $det(A-\lambda I)=0$:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}8-\lambda  & 9 \\ -4 & -4-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (8-\lambda )(-4-\lambda )-9\cdot (-4) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda -32+36 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +4 & =0 \\ (\lambda -2)(\lambda -2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=2.$ Since we get one repeated eigenvalue, the matrix might not be diagonalizable. To check this, we row-reduce the matrix $(A-2I)\text{x}=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 9 \\ -4 & -4\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6 & 9 \\ -4 & -6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+\frac{2}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}6 & 9 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has only $1$ pivot column. This implies that we will have only $2-1=1$ linearly independent eigenvector corresponding to the current eigenvalue. Therefore, $A$ is not diagonalizable.

questions.problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}7 & -8 \\ 4 & -5\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}∗ & 1 \\ ∗ & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $D={P}^{-1}AP,$   find the first column of the matrix $P.$
questions.worked_solution:
From the diagonal matrix $D=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]$, we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=3$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-1.$  

So, the first column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=3.$ 

Now, we simply need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{1}=3.$ Computing $A-3I,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}7 & -8 \\ 4 & -5\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -8 \\ 4 & -8\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -8 & 0 \\ 4 & -8 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}4 & -8 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=2{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}].$

questions.problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-3 & -1 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}∗ & 1 \\ ∗ & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $D={P}^{-1}AP,$   find the first column of the matrix $P.$
questions.worked_solution:
From the diagonal matrix $D=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]$, we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2.$  

So, the first column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=-1.$ 

Now, we simply need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{1}=-1.$ Computing $A-(-1)I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-1)I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & -1 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}]-(-1)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=2,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $P=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}].$

questions.problem: Find matrices $P$ and $D$ such that $PD{P}^{-1}=E,$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix and $E=[\begin{aligned}7 & 9 \\ -6 & -8\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
We apply the diagonalization algorithm. 

**Step 1.** We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix $E$ using its characteristic equation $det(E-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}7-\lambda  & 9 \\ -6 & -8-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (7-\lambda )(-8-\lambda )-9\cdot (-6) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+\lambda -2 & =0 \\ (\lambda -1)(\lambda +2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the eigenvalues of $E$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2.$

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $E.$

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}E-I & =[\begin{aligned}7 & 9 \\ -6 & -8\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6 & 9 \\ -6 & -9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}6 & 9 & 0 \\ -6 & -9 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}6 & 9 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-\frac{3}{2}{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=-2,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -2\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}E-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}7 & 9 \\ -6 & -8\end{aligned}]+2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}9 & 9 \\ -6 & -6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}9 & 9 & 0 \\ -6 & -6 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & ={R}_{2}+(\frac{2}{3}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}9 & 9 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

questions.problem:
Given the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}4 & -3 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]$, 
find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ such that $D={P}^{-1}AP.$
questions.worked_solution:
We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

**Step 1.**  We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix. Since matrix $A$ is triangular, its eigenvalues are the entries on the main diagonal:  

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=4\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}=1$

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-4I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -3 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -3 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}0 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

 
The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $2$nd one). Thus, ${x}_{1}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}=0.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -3 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -3 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a homogeneous system of linear equations with the matrix as above. Note, the matrix is already in row echelon form. There is one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is 

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ as follows: 

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Diagonalizing a 2x2 Matrix Given Its Eigenvalues

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Identifying Whether a Given 2x2 Matrix Is Diagonalizable
canonical_examples.problem:
Determine if the matrix
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/af05cedf7b2015f4f61df71e833390aa845d50126c3203369320ac6feb8b2cc3.svg)
is diagonalizable or not, and if it is diagonalizable, find a corresponding diagonal matrix $D.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Since $A$ is triangular, the eigenvalues are the entries on the main diagonal. 

So, the eigenvalues are $\lambda_1=\lambda_2=3.$ Since we get one repeated eigenvalue, the matrix might not be diagonalizable. To check this, we row-reduce the matrix $A-3I\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -5 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -5 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has only $1$ pivot column. This implies that we will have only $2-1=1$ linearly independent eigenvector corresponding to the current eigenvalue. Therefore, $A$ is not diagonalizable.

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Diagonalizing a 2x2 Matrix Given Part of the Diagonalization
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the following matrices:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/6e51c22c33c32d52c51657552a3c174d706a316ec10c78a4a953d2fcebc304ff.svg)
Given that $D=P^{-1}AP,$ find the value of $\dfrac{a}{b}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
From the diagonal matrix ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/0e25fe1b46b828e6fac168d1755af7aed9a7c3f657d1a6d6677fd71746b7ce31.svg) we deduce that the eigenvalues of $A$ are $\lambda_1=5$ and $\lambda_2=-1.$

So, the second column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda_2=-1.$ 

Now, we simply need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to $\lambda_2=-1.$ Computing $A-(-1)I,$ we get  

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-1)I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 2 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

To solve the corresponding system of linear equations, we construct the augmented matrix $M$ and reduce it to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & 0 \\ 2 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2}={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). So, $x_2$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain $x_1= -{2}x_2.$ Therefore, the general solution is

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/54dad1c9d747fead6f27dd0e9af7cca434c40a83d56c02c854bb610a1cdc6087.svg)

By setting $x_2=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/d28cf572126716928bc9ded7c2646871540e20b1d93d1efc929599b4c379d38b.svg)

Finally, $\dfrac{a}{b}=\dfrac{-2}{1} = -2.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Diagonalizing a 2x2 Matrix Given Part of the Diagonalization

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Diagonalizing a 2x2 Matrix
canonical_examples.problem:
Given the matrix 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/3da867d461c2b42c21badd67ce59c9ec5f6448597b4d2dcbb7e8b28ffe397768.svg) 
find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ such that $D=P^{-1}AP.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We apply the diagonalization algorithm. 

**Step 1.**  We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix. Since matrix $A$ is triangular, its eigenvalues are the entries on the main diagonal: 

$$
\lambda_1=3, \quad\quad\lambda_2=-2.
$$

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$

- For $\lambda_1=3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -8 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -8 \\ 0 & -5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

To solve the corresponding system of linear equations, we construct the augmented matrix $M$ and reduce it to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -8 & 0 \\ 0 & -5 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2}={R}_{2}+(-\frac{5}{8}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}0 & -8 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $2$nd one). So, $x_1$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain $x_2=0.$ Therefore, the general solution is
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/04f6efaa2bb141940040a04905e52aacd7aa739e1bd58dd71666a10543ff0f74.svg)
Setting $x_1=1,$ we get the eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/dd78cbf2025fdf012dc27429596c84be09825b436c32a5410f50f78cd4943a66.svg)

- For $\lambda_2=-2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -8 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]+2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & -8 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The above matrix corresponds to a homogeneous system of linear equations. Note, the matrix is already in row echelon form. There is one pivot column (the $1$st one). So, $x_2$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain $x_1=\dfrac{8}{5}x_2.$ Therefore, the general solution is
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/5b5b06d4cd243ca0370807b58bc9d0da68f34aa008956016bab3da29377df219.svg)
Setting  $x_2=5,$ we get the eigenvector  ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/3ea698aa474cb6d28b3fb511215fbe5da7d01b6653e884719d99483eac5635a0.svg)

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ as follows:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/b736228d68ad58b430f707236014be76e0354bf42ff9fcd73c495a077835bad7.svg)

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
A square matrix $A$ is called **diagonalizable** if there exists a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ such that

$$
A = PDP^{-1}.
$$

So, to **diagonalize** a matrix $A,$ we need to find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ that satisfy the equation above.

For example, let's diagonalize the matrix $A,$ given by

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/9dee6d9184932a79f36305b9fca2bbb5a2a18bc79b49ad97038f780a2f125e49.svg)

To diagonalize a $2\times 2$ matrix, we follow a three-step **diagonalization algorithm.**

**Step 1:** Find the eigenvalues of the matrix.

We solve the characteristic equation $\vert A - \lambda I \vert = 0.$ For the given matrix, the eigenvalues are $\color{red}\lambda_1 =2$ and $\color{blue}\lambda_2 =3.$

**Step 2:** Find a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ consisting of eigenvectors of the matrix.

Following the usual method for computing eigenvectors, we get 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/caa7716ce45eef38d92092d27827d30fd539fca27067c1e12f485a719b4f37ae.svg)

corresponding to the eigenvalues $\color{red}\lambda_1 =2$ and $\color{blue}\lambda_2 =3,$ respectively.

Note that $\left\{ {\color{red}\mathbf{v_1}}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{v_2}}\right\}$ is a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ since eigenvectors corresponding to distinct eigenvalues are linearly independent. This becomes important later.

**Step 3: ** Construct the matrices $D$ and $P.$

Now that we have our eigenvalues and corresponding eigenvectors, we can construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and invertible matrix $P.$

The matrix $D$ has the eigenvalues of the matrix as its entries on the diagonal. For now, we can write them in any order. So, we let

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/3e0df792d822773528cb07cceb39fcb98b7397ae70ab4f114e1450f1d91256d1.svg)

Then, the columns of $P$ are the corresponding eigenvectors. We need to write each eigenvector in the *same* column as its respective eigenvalue in the matrix $D.$ So, we get

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/869a05b6273dbbb1b53d9f842d8b2c612017517a0b007c1c5f494f55439a11b4.svg)

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A=PD{P}^{-1} & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can check our solution by computing the product on the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1} & =[\begin{aligned}6 & -6 \\ -2 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -6 \\ 1 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =A\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.title: Introduction
tutorials.content:
A square matrix $A$ is called **diagonalizable** if there exists a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ such that

$$
A = PDP^{-1}.
$$

So, to **diagonalize** a matrix $A,$ we need to find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ that satisfy the equation above.

For example, let's diagonalize the matrix $A,$ given by

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/9dee6d9184932a79f36305b9fca2bbb5a2a18bc79b49ad97038f780a2f125e49.svg)

To diagonalize a $2\times 2$ matrix, we follow a three-step **diagonalization algorithm.**

**Step 1:** Find the eigenvalues of the matrix.

We solve the characteristic equation $\vert A - \lambda I \vert = 0.$ For the given matrix, the eigenvalues are $\color{red}\lambda_1 =2$ and $\color{blue}\lambda_2 =3.$

**Step 2:** Find a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ consisting of eigenvectors of the matrix.

Following the usual method for computing eigenvectors, we get 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/caa7716ce45eef38d92092d27827d30fd539fca27067c1e12f485a719b4f37ae.svg)

corresponding to the eigenvalues $\color{red}\lambda_1 =2$ and $\color{blue}\lambda_2 =3,$ respectively.

Note that $\left\{ {\color{red}\mathbf{v_1}}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{v_2}}\right\}$ is a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ since eigenvectors corresponding to distinct eigenvalues are linearly independent. This becomes important later.

**Step 3: ** Construct the matrices $D$ and $P.$

Now that we have our eigenvalues and corresponding eigenvectors, we can construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and invertible matrix $P.$

The matrix $D$ has the eigenvalues of the matrix as its entries on the diagonal. For now, we can write them in any order. So, we let

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/3e0df792d822773528cb07cceb39fcb98b7397ae70ab4f114e1450f1d91256d1.svg)

Then, the columns of $P$ are the corresponding eigenvectors. We need to write each eigenvector in the *same* column as its respective eigenvalue in the matrix $D.$ So, we get

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/869a05b6273dbbb1b53d9f842d8b2c612017517a0b007c1c5f494f55439a11b4.svg)

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A=PD{P}^{-1} & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can check our solution by computing the product on the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1} & =[\begin{aligned}6 & -6 \\ -2 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -6 \\ 1 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =A\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Diagonalizable vs. Non-Diagonalizable Matrices
tutorials.problem:
There is a theorem that states the following:

*If $A$ is a $2 \times 2$ matrix, then it is diagonalizable if and only if there exists a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ that consists of eigenvectors of $A.$*

We can break this down into two possible cases:

- If $A$ has two distinct eigenvalues, then it is indeed diagonalizable. This is because two distinct eigenvalues will give rise to two linearly independent eigenvectors (one for each eigenvalue). 

So, for a matrix $A$ with eigenvalues $\color{red}\lambda_1$ and $\color{blue}\lambda_2$ and corresponding eigenvectors $\color{red}\mathbf{v_1}$ and $\color{blue}\mathbf{v_2},$ we have
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/e1468bc5ccdff43e33587c7b4b500bc527ab0ac7e74410ea53df1f803a19b520.svg)

tutorials.title: Diagonalizable vs. Non-Diagonalizable Matrices
tutorials.content:
There is a theorem that states the following:

*If $A$ is a $2 \times 2$ matrix, then it is diagonalizable if and only if there exists a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ that consists of eigenvectors of $A.$*

We can break this down into two possible cases:

- If $A$ has two distinct eigenvalues, then it is indeed diagonalizable. This is because two distinct eigenvalues will give rise to two linearly independent eigenvectors (one for each eigenvalue). 

So, for a matrix $A$ with eigenvalues $\color{red}\lambda_1$ and $\color{blue}\lambda_2$ and corresponding eigenvectors $\color{red}\mathbf{v_1}$ and $\color{blue}\mathbf{v_2},$ we have
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/e1468bc5ccdff43e33587c7b4b500bc527ab0ac7e74410ea53df1f803a19b520.svg)

- If we get a double root $\lambda$ of the characteristic equation, the matrix will be diagonalizable *only if* we can find exactly two linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to $\lambda,$ which may or may not be possible. Another way of saying this is that the corresponding eigenspace $V_\lambda$ must be of dimension $2.$

tutorials.name: The Connection Between a Matrix and Its Diagonal Form
tutorials.problem:
If $A$ is a diagonalizable matrix, then we can write

$$
A=PDP^{-1}.
$$

 

We can write this equation in an equivalent form, making $D$ the subject.

First, we left-multiply both sides of the equation by $P^{-1}\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =PD{P}^{-1} \\ {P}^{-1}\cdot A & ={P}^{-1}\cdot PD{P}^{-1} \\ {P}^{-1}A & ={I}_{2}D{P}^{-1} \\ {P}^{-1}A & =D{P}^{-1}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we right-multiply both sides of the equation by $P{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{-1}A\cdot P & =D{P}^{-1}\cdot P \\ {P}^{-1}AP & =D{I}_{2} \\ {P}^{-1}AP & =D\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
A=PDP^{-1}
\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
D = P^{-1}A P.
$$

tutorials.name: Uniqueness of the Diagonalization
tutorials.problem:
Given a matrix $A,$ the diagonalization 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/76843143729d2bc62fc74dc6f03c24eb6a12dfc16a2609a8f2b36499cf39ce90.svg)

is almost unique, but not quite.

When we construct the diagonal matrix $D,$ we can put the eigenvalues in any order. So this matrix is unique up to permutations of the order of the eigenvalues. Note that by swapping the eigenvalues in $D,$ we then have to swap the corresponding eigenvectors (columns) in $P{:}$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/dec5fece3d89eaa022b4e951e63259b0f87213997397b1f8a91fb8fdabed0f74.svg)

Also, since any non-zero multiple of an eigenvector is an eigenvector as well, the eigenvector basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ can consist of these multiples instead. So the invertible matrix $P$ is unique up to multiples of its columns.

tutorials.title: Uniqueness of the Diagonalization
tutorials.content:
Given a matrix $A,$ the diagonalization 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/76843143729d2bc62fc74dc6f03c24eb6a12dfc16a2609a8f2b36499cf39ce90.svg)

is almost unique, but not quite.

When we construct the diagonal matrix $D,$ we can put the eigenvalues in any order. So this matrix is unique up to permutations of the order of the eigenvalues. Note that by swapping the eigenvalues in $D,$ we then have to swap the corresponding eigenvectors (columns) in $P{:}$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/dec5fece3d89eaa022b4e951e63259b0f87213997397b1f8a91fb8fdabed0f74.svg)

Also, since any non-zero multiple of an eigenvector is an eigenvector as well, the eigenvector basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ can consist of these multiples instead. So the invertible matrix $P$ is unique up to multiples of its columns.

tutorials.name: Diagonalization as a Change of Coordinates
tutorials.problem:
Let ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/3207697e43e4f88223ad85c16964c3103a50c0c999a4ca14417695158d45526b.svg) be a diagonalizable ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/2521651122403a440e682fef383af333958f5b0d1334abe8b0771865d4daf100.svg) matrix. Then we can write
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/d8f75220bef8327a8dfc49a6ae22e79c6f1649aefdc8fb43065e0616975a8c5c.svg)
where

- ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/1aaddf0d4be4d873ff6c0600b0b239e0565a05ca8daaff7ca92bd5c70bebcf03.svg) is an invertible matrix whose columns are eigenvectors ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/13cfebc7f22b3c6cfe7a66492040f9c7682e27e72b0a9adbc033e6a815c68fd9.svg) and ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/d0c6e1eed1577bd5d71e38657d494bf53798b9c1f52c54e4a270e200df1cc351.svg) of ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/c2c85081d1f89d74b8ebb2761496d211d7052193809b7864e7983437f5d0b80f.svg) and

- ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/5914524b1d3db63c66998b75ca1d00a5dc4e294d2a8f10fe384d2b2ebf2af38e.svg) is a diagonal matrix whose diagonal entries are the corresponding eigenvalues ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/ff5243fdeda78658220d1bcd4ac9b5963157b5e1f8b6a31231c68a6743248b19.svg) and ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/4a2dd44cea07e06ccec03fff120c7fdbcebe19ad7a31d8abde1ab95c8a6b53a1.svg)

To understand this better, we need to distinguish between two coordinate systems.

In ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/fb3130e489fdca80d1a077702861c20532fe613f9942d48fa1ec24055494a383.svg) the **standard basis** is
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/d29d3ee4ae42a8d4ee5304cb0d29c6c811838d7b893a3a831b1b1b8b3af12561.svg)

So, if a vector is written as
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/bbbc0379f1691a30dec4c34ec6171db1f116bec12a24891169957af68164f8d3.svg)
then ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/12adb8ba7ed45d89c9d9a80eb7c06616c41999e9fac57732bc24d2b55e1f8073.svg) The numbers ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/349015631ec44ef653936c85586d2c5ef56ba64392b3f92b4b92cbef3e731bc5.svg) and ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/a77a353782459b753313d80235712695d65dc4a44d8d357aa41add6729f81d8f.svg) are the *standard coordinates* of ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/1f3d1a60926323e963d7563529669e5cf8210771c8cbb0379f7a7d90e7c6aeec.svg)

Now let
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/58cdfb66e4c93d643fb97273610b3bbf67c8831516d4ccfc5b7790d55a169b28.svg)

Since the columns of ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/1aaddf0d4be4d873ff6c0600b0b239e0565a05ca8daaff7ca92bd5c70bebcf03.svg) are ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/13cfebc7f22b3c6cfe7a66492040f9c7682e27e72b0a9adbc033e6a815c68fd9.svg) and ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/d0c6e1eed1577bd5d71e38657d494bf53798b9c1f52c54e4a270e200df1cc351.svg) written in standard coordinates, the matrix ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/1aaddf0d4be4d873ff6c0600b0b239e0565a05ca8daaff7ca92bd5c70bebcf03.svg) converts coordinates from the basis ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/be2d796b77bebb31c0c06cef6af82bc9fb606a584a52cc5385cd32c4e143236c.svg) to the standard basis.

So, for any vector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/b2cb236f7a7f426f303b1391f76900b47f7d2fa1ad9c8110d8584182559017fd.svg)
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/7e5a6a4b9bee9550e68c75a3945ad25d41f1de6dd3b089ce89005428da169f9d.svg)

Here, ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/4fa2300af121b336bb0d7845b8e2b3e34be5a517a1bca45b4ec7b6514b2c544d.svg) denotes the standard-coordinate column of the vector, while ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/3f7132e53e5a27bee4c84bdddbac07971ec44ce12539c0e0c23bf0006057e199.svg) denotes the coordinate column of the same vector in the eigenvector basis ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/8d16f7d70344ddea7a4fe48105e5ea75b984f48fd77f6f6eb89d26ad91b65805.svg)

Also, in the basis ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/dab6f1afbeb705eef0eaf1a338c977e9cf6578010ebf95a6fccd1a4a4610dcd4.svg) the eigenvectors have especially simple coordinate columns:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/9f5fec87a4253a3a1741c3380e2c6f9331928883ab2083dc02bf0e8efda6a98a.svg)

This is because
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/306d2bb3211dac2883b1eb6abaed54259272a8bcc6a4e562ff5da6fc52dee520.svg)

So, in the basis ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/dab6f1afbeb705eef0eaf1a338c977e9cf6578010ebf95a6fccd1a4a4610dcd4.svg) the matrix ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/5914524b1d3db63c66998b75ca1d00a5dc4e294d2a8f10fe384d2b2ebf2af38e.svg) acts by scaling the first coordinate by ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/ff5243fdeda78658220d1bcd4ac9b5963157b5e1f8b6a31231c68a6743248b19.svg) and the second coordinate by ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/4a2dd44cea07e06ccec03fff120c7fdbcebe19ad7a31d8abde1ab95c8a6b53a1.svg)

We can summarize this process for any vector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/4fa2300af121b336bb0d7845b8e2b3e34be5a517a1bca45b4ec7b6514b2c544d.svg) as a sequence of three steps:

- first, rewrite ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/4fa2300af121b336bb0d7845b8e2b3e34be5a517a1bca45b4ec7b6514b2c544d.svg) in the eigenvector basis ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/dab6f1afbeb705eef0eaf1a338c977e9cf6578010ebf95a6fccd1a4a4610dcd4.svg)

- then, apply the diagonal matrix ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/5914524b1d3db63c66998b75ca1d00a5dc4e294d2a8f10fe384d2b2ebf2af38e.svg) in that basis,

- finally, convert the result back to standard coordinates.

The diagram below shows this sequence.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/1459b0643f99c186f9710118617f89f34a601526e7154213471404d2feb2aaeb.svg)

tutorials.title: Diagonalization as a Change of Coordinates
tutorials.content:
Let ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/3207697e43e4f88223ad85c16964c3103a50c0c999a4ca14417695158d45526b.svg) be a diagonalizable ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/2521651122403a440e682fef383af333958f5b0d1334abe8b0771865d4daf100.svg) matrix. Then we can write
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/d8f75220bef8327a8dfc49a6ae22e79c6f1649aefdc8fb43065e0616975a8c5c.svg)
where

- ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/1aaddf0d4be4d873ff6c0600b0b239e0565a05ca8daaff7ca92bd5c70bebcf03.svg) is an invertible matrix whose columns are eigenvectors ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/13cfebc7f22b3c6cfe7a66492040f9c7682e27e72b0a9adbc033e6a815c68fd9.svg) and ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/d0c6e1eed1577bd5d71e38657d494bf53798b9c1f52c54e4a270e200df1cc351.svg) of ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/c2c85081d1f89d74b8ebb2761496d211d7052193809b7864e7983437f5d0b80f.svg) and

- ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/5914524b1d3db63c66998b75ca1d00a5dc4e294d2a8f10fe384d2b2ebf2af38e.svg) is a diagonal matrix whose diagonal entries are the corresponding eigenvalues ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/ff5243fdeda78658220d1bcd4ac9b5963157b5e1f8b6a31231c68a6743248b19.svg) and ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/4a2dd44cea07e06ccec03fff120c7fdbcebe19ad7a31d8abde1ab95c8a6b53a1.svg)

To understand this better, we need to distinguish between two coordinate systems.

In ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/fb3130e489fdca80d1a077702861c20532fe613f9942d48fa1ec24055494a383.svg) the **standard basis** is
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/d29d3ee4ae42a8d4ee5304cb0d29c6c811838d7b893a3a831b1b1b8b3af12561.svg)

So, if a vector is written as
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/bbbc0379f1691a30dec4c34ec6171db1f116bec12a24891169957af68164f8d3.svg)
then ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/12adb8ba7ed45d89c9d9a80eb7c06616c41999e9fac57732bc24d2b55e1f8073.svg) The numbers ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/349015631ec44ef653936c85586d2c5ef56ba64392b3f92b4b92cbef3e731bc5.svg) and ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/a77a353782459b753313d80235712695d65dc4a44d8d357aa41add6729f81d8f.svg) are the *standard coordinates* of ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/1f3d1a60926323e963d7563529669e5cf8210771c8cbb0379f7a7d90e7c6aeec.svg)

Now let
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/58cdfb66e4c93d643fb97273610b3bbf67c8831516d4ccfc5b7790d55a169b28.svg)

Since the columns of ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/1aaddf0d4be4d873ff6c0600b0b239e0565a05ca8daaff7ca92bd5c70bebcf03.svg) are ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/13cfebc7f22b3c6cfe7a66492040f9c7682e27e72b0a9adbc033e6a815c68fd9.svg) and ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/d0c6e1eed1577bd5d71e38657d494bf53798b9c1f52c54e4a270e200df1cc351.svg) written in standard coordinates, the matrix ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/1aaddf0d4be4d873ff6c0600b0b239e0565a05ca8daaff7ca92bd5c70bebcf03.svg) converts coordinates from the basis ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/be2d796b77bebb31c0c06cef6af82bc9fb606a584a52cc5385cd32c4e143236c.svg) to the standard basis.

So, for any vector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/b2cb236f7a7f426f303b1391f76900b47f7d2fa1ad9c8110d8584182559017fd.svg)
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/7e5a6a4b9bee9550e68c75a3945ad25d41f1de6dd3b089ce89005428da169f9d.svg)

Here, ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/4fa2300af121b336bb0d7845b8e2b3e34be5a517a1bca45b4ec7b6514b2c544d.svg) denotes the standard-coordinate column of the vector, while ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/3f7132e53e5a27bee4c84bdddbac07971ec44ce12539c0e0c23bf0006057e199.svg) denotes the coordinate column of the same vector in the eigenvector basis ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/8d16f7d70344ddea7a4fe48105e5ea75b984f48fd77f6f6eb89d26ad91b65805.svg)

Also, in the basis ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/dab6f1afbeb705eef0eaf1a338c977e9cf6578010ebf95a6fccd1a4a4610dcd4.svg) the eigenvectors have especially simple coordinate columns:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/9f5fec87a4253a3a1741c3380e2c6f9331928883ab2083dc02bf0e8efda6a98a.svg)

This is because
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/306d2bb3211dac2883b1eb6abaed54259272a8bcc6a4e562ff5da6fc52dee520.svg)

So, in the basis ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/dab6f1afbeb705eef0eaf1a338c977e9cf6578010ebf95a6fccd1a4a4610dcd4.svg) the matrix ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/5914524b1d3db63c66998b75ca1d00a5dc4e294d2a8f10fe384d2b2ebf2af38e.svg) acts by scaling the first coordinate by ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/ff5243fdeda78658220d1bcd4ac9b5963157b5e1f8b6a31231c68a6743248b19.svg) and the second coordinate by ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/4a2dd44cea07e06ccec03fff120c7fdbcebe19ad7a31d8abde1ab95c8a6b53a1.svg)

We can summarize this process for any vector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/4fa2300af121b336bb0d7845b8e2b3e34be5a517a1bca45b4ec7b6514b2c544d.svg) as a sequence of three steps:

- first, rewrite ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/4fa2300af121b336bb0d7845b8e2b3e34be5a517a1bca45b4ec7b6514b2c544d.svg) in the eigenvector basis ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/dab6f1afbeb705eef0eaf1a338c977e9cf6578010ebf95a6fccd1a4a4610dcd4.svg)

- then, apply the diagonal matrix ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/5914524b1d3db63c66998b75ca1d00a5dc4e294d2a8f10fe384d2b2ebf2af38e.svg) in that basis,

- finally, convert the result back to standard coordinates.

The diagram below shows this sequence.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14130997/assets/1459b0643f99c186f9710118617f89f34a601526e7154213471404d2feb2aaeb.svg)

There is a theorem that states the following:

If is a matrix, then it is diagonalizable if and only if there exists a basis of that consists of eigenvectors of

steps.title: Uniqueness of the Diagonalization
steps.html:
Uniqueness of the Diagonalization
?

Given a matrix the diagonalization

is almost unique, but not quite.

When we construct the diagonal matrix we can put the eigenvalues in any order. So this matrix is unique up to permutations of the order of the eigenvalues. Note that by swapping the eigenvalues in we then have to swap the corresponding eigenvectors (columns) in

Also, since any non-zero multiple of an eigenvector is an eigenvector as well, the eigenvector basis of can consist of these multiples instead. So the invertible matrix is unique up to multiples of its columns.
